questions.stem: Where does the right ventricle send blood?

options.text: To the body
options.rationale: That is the left ventricle's job.

options.text: To the lungs
options.rationale: Correct — the right side supplies the pulmonary circulation.

options.text: To the left atrium directly
options.rationale: Blood reaches the left atrium via the lungs.

options.text: To the coronary arteries
options.rationale: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta.

questions.stem: Why is the left ventricle thicker than the right?

options.text: Because it holds more blood
options.rationale: Wall thickness reflects pressure generated, not volume held.

options.text: Because it must generate enough pressure to supply the whole body
options.rationale: Correct. Wall thickness tracks the pressure a chamber has to generate.

options.text: Because it beats more often
options.rationale: Both ventricles beat at the same rate.

options.text: Because it contains the conduction system
options.rationale: The conduction system runs through both.

questions.stem: If the left side of the heart fails, where does blood back up?

options.text: Into the lungs
options.rationale: Correct — which is why left-sided failure causes pulmonary congestion.

options.text: Into the legs and abdomen
options.rationale: That is the pattern of right-sided failure.

options.text: Into the coronary arteries
options.rationale: Coronary flow is not where backpressure accumulates.

options.text: Nowhere; failure does not cause backpressure
options.rationale: Backpressure is the mechanism of congestion.

questions.stem: Which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker?

options.text: The atrioventricular node
options.rationale: The AV node is a backup site, not the normal pacemaker.

options.text: The sinoatrial node
options.rationale: Correct — it fires fastest and therefore sets the pace.

options.text: The left ventricle
options.rationale: The ventricles are not the normal origin of the impulse.

options.text: The vagus nerve
options.rationale: The vagus influences rate but does not generate the impulse.

questions.stem: Why does the atrioventricular node delay the impulse?

options.text: To allow the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles
options.rationale: Correct — the pause is deliberate and improves filling.

options.text: To slow the overall heart rate
options.rationale: Rate is set by the pacemaker site, not by this delay.

options.text: To protect the conduction fibres
options.rationale: Protection is not the purpose of the delay.

options.text: It is a fault that occurs with age
options.rationale: The delay is a normal design feature.

questions.stem: A monitor shows an organised rhythm. What does this establish?

options.text: That the patient has a pulse
options.rationale: Electrical activity does not establish mechanical output.

options.text: That the electrical system is producing impulses, nothing more
options.rationale: Correct — you still check a pulse.

options.text: That cardiac output is adequate
options.rationale: Output cannot be inferred from the tracing.

options.text: That CPR can be stopped
options.rationale: Stopping compressions on a rhythm alone would be an error.

questions.verify_notes: Written from standard EMT curriculum (AAOS Emergency Care 12e level); not reviewed against a source text. Confirm the fact tested and every option's rationale against the source, then add a source reference.

options.rationale: Correct — the volume moved per minute.

options.text: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
options.rationale: That is not the relationship.

options.text: The pressure in the aorta
options.rationale: That is blood pressure, a different quantity.

options.text: The volume of the left ventricle
options.rationale: Chamber volume is not output.

options.rationale: That is afterload.

options.text: How full the ventricle is before it contracts
options.rationale: Correct. Preload is the filling; afterload is the resistance.

options.text: The thickness of the ventricular wall
options.rationale: Wall thickness is a structural property.

options.text: The rate at which the ventricle contracts
options.rationale: Rate is a separate variable.

questions.stem: Why is tachycardia an early sign of shock?

options.text: Because the heart is inflamed
options.rationale: Inflammation is not the mechanism.

options.text: Because the body raises rate to maintain output as stroke volume falls
options.rationale: Correct — and it does so long before blood pressure moves.

options.text: Because pain always raises heart rate
options.rationale: Pain can, but that is not the shock mechanism.

options.text: Because blood pressure has already fallen
options.rationale: Blood pressure typically has not fallen yet at this stage.

questions.stem: Why does a very high heart rate eventually reduce cardiac output?

options.text: Because the heart muscle tires immediately
options.rationale: Fatigue is not the described mechanism.

options.text: Because there is too little time between beats for the ventricle to fill
options.rationale: Correct — filling happens in the gaps.

options.text: Because the valves stop working above a certain rate
options.rationale: Valve failure is not the mechanism.

options.text: Because afterload falls to zero
options.rationale: Afterload does not fall to zero.

questions.stem: Where do the coronary arteries arise?

options.text: From the pulmonary artery
options.rationale: They arise from the aorta, not the pulmonary artery.

options.text: From the aorta, immediately after it leaves the left ventricle
options.rationale: Correct — the heart takes its supply first.

options.text: From the right atrium
options.rationale: Arteries do not arise from an atrium.

options.text: From the inferior vena cava
options.rationale: That is a vein returning blood to the heart.

questions.stem: When do the coronary arteries fill?

options.text: During contraction, when pressure is highest
options.rationale: Contraction compresses the vessels and limits flow.

options.text: Mainly between beats, when the muscle relaxes
options.rationale: Correct — which is why tachycardia reduces coronary filling time.

options.text: Continuously and equally throughout the cycle
options.rationale: Flow is not equal across the cycle.

options.text: Only during deep inspiration
options.rationale: Respiration is not what drives coronary filling.

questions.stem: What happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked?

options.text: The whole heart stops immediately
options.rationale: A blockage affects a territory, not necessarily the whole heart at once.

options.text: The muscle downstream of the blockage is starved of oxygen
options.rationale: Correct — that is a myocardial infarction.

options.text: Blood is rerouted through the chambers
options.rationale: The chambers do not supply the muscle.

options.text: The conduction system takes over the blood supply
options.rationale: Conduction tissue does not supply blood.
